text:
*Disgusting:* causing strong feelings of dislike, revulsion, or disgust.

Now, about the title *“iPhone Duo pricing is disgusting in India.”*

No. What is ridiculous here is the sense of entitlement behind that statement.

I’m Indian too, and this needs to be said plainly: *Apple does not owe Indians an affordable iPhone Duo.*

Nobody is forcing you to buy it. It isn't food, medicine, housing, or a basic necessity. It is a $1,999 foldable luxury smartphone from a company worth roughly **$4.6 trillion**.

Apple decided what its product costs. You have exactly the same freedom to decide whether that price is worth paying.

Can afford it and think it's worth the money? *Buy it.*

Can't afford it, or think the value is terrible? *Don't buy it.*

That's how a voluntary consumer market works.

Call it **expensive**. Call it **overpriced**. Say it's **terrible value for Indian buyers**. Compare it with Samsung or other foldables and explain why the competition offers more for less. Those are legitimate criticisms.

But calling the pricing *“disgusting”* as though Apple has some obligation to price its most expensive foldable around Indian purchasing power is absurd.

India is an important and rapidly growing market for Apple, but **the world does not revolve around the Indian consumer**. Apple sells globally. It does not need every Indian—or every American, Australian, Briton, European, or anyone else—to be able to afford every product it makes.

A Mercedes being unaffordable to most Indians doesn't make Mercedes “disgusting.” A luxury watch being unaffordable doesn't make its manufacturer “disgusting.” The same principle applies here.

And there's another fact being conveniently ignored: India's retail price isn't simply money Apple pockets. *Indian taxes and other local market costs contribute to the higher Indian price.* So if you're going to analyze the India/U.S. difference, analyze the actual components instead of turning the thumbnail into outrage bait.

The iPhone Duo is a premium, optional consumer product. *You are not entitled to it at a price you personally consider affordable.*

Review the specifications. Question the value. Compare the competition. Criticize Apple's decisions as aggressively as the facts justify.

But don't confuse *“I don't like the price”* with *“the price is disgusting.”*

Those are two completely different statements.

And please spare us the manufactured outrage. *Nobody is forcing anybody to buy an iPhone Duo. If the price makes no sense to you, don't buy it. That's the strongest message a consumer can send.*

text: People hyping the iPhone Duo really need to look past showroom marketing and research the actual wave physics, thermodynamics, and mechanical compromises behind it. Acoustically, even when unfolded completely flat at 180°, you don’t get a true, coherent stereo image: because internal components are asymmetrical (motherboard and camera cluster on one half, battery layout on the other), the drivers are forced into a staggered, diagonal axis with mismatched back-volumes. Under wave physics, this creates unequal acoustic compliance, group delay discrepancies, and direct path-length differences that trigger destructive phase cancellation and comb filtering before the sound reaches your ears, with your palms inevitably choking the grilles in landscape anyway. Thermally, pairing an external titanium frame—which has roughly one-tenth the thermal conductivity of aluminum—with a razor-thin micro vapor chamber makes zero physical sense. With such a microscopic fluid volume, that chamber hits dry-out and thermal saturation almost immediately under sustained loads, while the insulating titanium frame traps the heat inside around the SoC, battery, and folding adhesives instead of rejecting it outward. Add an exposed nano-texture display where repeated swiping across the crease will permanently burnish the etched micro-ridges into an uneven, glossy strip with zero sacrificial screen protectors available to replace, and running an unyielding, rigid Apple Pencil tip over that same fragile etched glass will concentrate massive point-load shear stress, permanently grooving the surface and crushing the micro-crests. The whole design is a series of flawed engineering trade-offs.

In italiano, davanti alle parole maschili che iniziano con una "s" seguita da consonante (la cosiddetta s impura), si usano gli articoli lo al singolare e gli al plurale.

Quando si italianizzano termini inglesi al volo durante un discorso veloce, viene spontaneo appiccicarci l'articolo plurale più comune ("i"), ma rimane un errore.

2017–2019 — sticker price creeps up in the UK even when the US dollar price stays at $999, mostly FX / VAT positioning. 11 Pro is the first named Pro and the first UK Pro over £1,000.
2020 — charger and EarPods gone. Phone price dips £50, storage floor doubles.
2021 — another £50 cut on the Pro. Cheapest Pro launch of the whole run: £949.
2022 — the ugly year. Weak pound + inflation. Pro jumps £150 to £1,099 even though the US dollar price stayed $999.
2023–2024 — Apple walks the UK Pro back to £999 and holds it for two years. Pro Max stays £1,199 but the Max’s cheapest tier becomes 256GB.
2025 — Pro goes to £1,099 and the cheap 128GB Pro disappears. Same dollar/pound number, more storage.
2026 (announced 9 Sept 2026) — another £100 on both Pro and Pro Max: £1,199 / £1,299.

I had a Samsung folding phone. It was great for what it was. However, the screen malfunctioned within a year (and had to be replaced). However, I decided that I could buy a Samsung Galaxy tablet AND the Galaxy S26 Ultra -- for less money than the folding Galaxy Z Fold.

I suspect that the same is probably true with the Apple folding devices (this one and any in the future). $2000 is a heck of a lot of money to spend on a phone that doesn't have the specs of the iPhone Pro Max. I do like that Apple are locking down further on the fact that the Pro phones are aimed at performance and function first. I genuinely feel like my phone is a true B-cam/complimentary camera to my main camera.

The larger vapor chamber is nice, as the one in my 17 PM combined with that “hated” aluminum body, has personally allowed for me to stay out in the field longer, and get a lot more work done. I do love the three activities feature that the smaller Dynamic Island has now; that was a highlight for me. Ultimately, of course, my 17 Pro Max won’t be seeing me upgrading from it, but the 18 Pros are a nice little refinement of this form factor. The camera upgrades are minor, with the Ultra Wide lens having still not received an update, and the tele lens understandably not getting an upgrade since I got a massive one last year.

If one is one a 14 Pro or earlier, then the 18s will be a pretty massive jump.

text:
First, Apple put a great deal of effort into launching its first foldable device, the "iPhone Duo," aiming for a high level of refinement—perhaps even more than initially expected—and the reception has been quite positive.

However, regarding the screen crease, the iPhone Duo has a crease comparable to that of the Z8. While it isn't very noticeable when the screen is on, it becomes visible against the black background when the screen is turned off. To make the crease less conspicuous, Apple applied an anti-fingerprint matte film they call "Nano-texture." While this matte film minimizes light reflection and makes the crease much less visible, it has drawn complaints for making video content appear less sharp and text look more blurred compared to the Z Fold. In short, there is a trade-off involved.
Additionally, the display used in the iPhone is supplied by Samsung Display (a Samsung subsidiary) and is a newly released, cutting-edge model; this same display will likely be used in the upcoming Samsung Z9 as well.

Regarding the "Flex Mode" mentioned at the 7:47 mark: using the "GripTok" accessory shown in the video allows the device to function in "laptop mode." Furthermore, by downloading specific apps from the Google Play Store, users can enable a Flex Mode control panel or a laptop-style keyboard on the bottom half of the screen. In other words, this functionality is entirely possible on the Z8 as well via software apps. However, using the bottom display as a keyboard in laptop mode has limited practicality due to issues regarding size and the risk of scratching the screen. It would actually be far more practical to buy a Bluetooth mini-keyboard for around $20 and type on the unfolded Z Fold screen while propping the device up with a GripTok. Therefore, Apple’s "Flex Mode" or "Laptop Mode" doesn't really offer a significant advantage. While applying a matte film might make the crease less visible, it could end up being a drawback rather than a benefit if it compromises image clarity or causes text to appear noticeably more blurred. Furthermore, the added film pushes the total weight up to 254g; holding the device for extended periods while watching videos or browsing the web in bed would put considerable strain on your wrist.
